hero.headline: Oil Prices Rise After U.S. and Iran Exchange Military Strikes
hero.body:
The United States carried out new strikes on Iranian military targets, including a ground control station in Bandar Abbas, while also shooting down four Iranian attack drones near the Strait of Hormuz. The military action prompted what appeared to be a retaliatory strike from Iran on an American airbase in Kuwait, marking another escalation in the ongoing conflict between the two nations.

U.S. Central Command forces intercepted the Iranian drones that posed a threat around the strait. According to U.S. officials, the strikes were "measured, purely defensive, and intended to maintain the ceasefire." Two hours after the American strikes, Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed they had targeted the American base in Kuwait in response. Kuwait confirmed its air defenses were intercepting hostile missile and drone threats early Thursday morning.

The confrontation also extended to commercial shipping. Iranian forces fired at four vessels attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz without coordination with security forces, according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, though no details were provided about the ships or any damage.

Oil prices spiked in reaction to the military exchange as traders assessed risks to global energy supplies flowing from the Persian Gulf region. However, markets showed some restraint after President Trump indicated that negotiations with Iran were continuing, creating volatility throughout the trading session. Bond yields also climbed as investors repositioned portfolios in response to the geopolitical uncertainty.

The fresh strikes came as Trump made combative statements about Iran and the strait. At a White House cabinet meeting, Trump said "Either that or we'll have to just finish the job" regarding Iran negotiations, claiming Iran was "negotiating on fumes." He also appeared to direct a warning at Oman, a U.S. ally, regarding control of the Strait of Hormuz, saying it would be "open to everybody" and that "Oman will behave just like everybody else or we'll have to blow them up."

A key unresolved issue in ceasefire talks involves whether any agreement will cover Israel's military operations against Hezbollah in Lebanon. Iran has insisted Lebanon must be included in any ceasefire agreement. Meanwhile, Israeli forces have intensified operations in Lebanon, with the military striking 550 targets since the beginning of the week and Israeli troops pushing farther north into the country.

Stock markets ultimately closed higher despite the oil price surge, with major indexes reaching record levels. Technology stocks helped offset concerns about rising energy costs, and the Nasdaq also hit new highs. Investors appeared to take some comfort from Trump's indication that negotiations remained active, even as both countries continued military posturing.

The situation remains uncertain as the U.S. and Iran maintain both military confrontation and diplomatic channels. Energy markets are likely to remain sensitive to developments in both military movements and negotiation status as traders weigh the risks of further escalation against the possibility of diplomatic resolution.

cards.headline: Russian ballistic missiles strike Kyiv, killing at least five
cards.body:
Russian forces launched a massive assault on Kyiv using hypersonic and ballistic missiles, killing at least four people and wounding approximately 100 across the country, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The attack involved around 600 drones and 90 missiles of various types, including 36 ballistic missiles. Russia employed its Oreshnik hypersonic missile for the third time in the conflict, along with Iskander, Kinzhal and Zircon missiles. The Russian defense ministry claimed the strikes targeted military command facilities, airbases and weapons factories, but most damage occurred in civilian areas.

Kyiv bore the brunt of the assault, with Zelenskyy noting that not all ballistic missiles were intercepted. The capital's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, reported two people killed and 56 wounded in the city itself. Two additional deaths occurred in the surrounding Kyiv region, with nine wounded. Damage extended across every district of Kyiv, affecting residential buildings, schools and commercial centers.

The attack damaged several significant structures. Ukraine's National Art Museum, which houses one of the country's largest collections, sustained damage including broken windows and debris scattered throughout. The culture ministry stated the actual collection remained safe. Ukraine's foreign ministry building, struck for the first time since World War II, suffered light damage from nearby explosions. Government headquarters also had windows blown out but no injuries resulted.

A fire broke out at a school hit during the strikes. Another attack on a business center left people trapped in a shelter. In Bila Tserkva in the Kyiv region, Russian missiles destroyed a market and damaged a water supply facility. One market worker told the Associated Press she planned to leave Kyiv after 22 years of employment, saying "everything has burned down."

A 74-year-old Kyiv resident described being thrown back by shock waves when explosions occurred near his apartment. "My apartment was blown to pieces," he said, though he and his dog survived.

Russia's defense ministry claimed the attack was retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory. Ukraine's ambassador rejected accusations of war crimes at a UN Security Council emergency meeting called by Russia, describing the session as "pure propaganda."

International leaders condemned the strikes. French President Emmanuel Macron said the Oreshnik missile use signaled "the dead end of Russia's war of aggression." German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called it "reckless escalation." European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the attacks as "abhorrent acts of terror meant to kill as many civilians as possible," adding that the Oreshnik use represented "political scare tactic and reckless nuclear brinkmanship."

Culture Minister Tetyana Berezhna stated Russia was "systematically attacking civilian infrastructure and cultural institutions" as an attempt "to intimidate and destroy our identity."

cards.headline: Defense Secretary Hegseth removes female and Black Navy officers from promotion list
cards.teaser: Pete Hegseth struck certain officers from a Navy promotion list based on gender and race.
cards.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed female and Black officers from a Navy promotion list, according to The New York Times. The action by Hegseth affects officers who were slated for advancement within the naval service.

The removals represent a departure from standard military promotion procedures, which typically rely on performance evaluations and time in service. The decision has drawn attention to how personnel decisions are being made at the Pentagon under the current administration.

cards.headline: Appeals court blocks Trump transgender military ban as unconstitutional
cards.body:
A federal appeals court ruled on Monday that the Trump administration is unconstitutionally expelling active transgender troops under a policy implemented by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The divided three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for Washington DC delivered a significant legal setback to the administration's efforts to remove transgender service members from the military.

The majority opinion characterized the ban as "arbitrary, and based on animus," according to the court's decision. However, the split ruling also allows the armed services to continue blocking transgender individuals from enlisting in the military, creating a distinction between active duty personnel and new recruits.

The court's decision is expected to face challenges from the government, with legal experts predicting the case will ultimately reach the Supreme Court. The ruling represents a complex outcome that restricts the scope of the administration's transgender military policy while leaving room for future legal battles over enlistment restrictions.

Hegseth responded to the ruling by signaling his intention to appeal to the nation's highest court. In a statement following the decision, he wrote "see you at SCOTUS," indicating his willingness to pursue the case further through the judicial system.

The case has become a focal point in the broader debate over the Trump administration's anti-diversity agenda. Civil liberties advocates have argued that the policy unconstitutionally targets transgender service members, while the administration has maintained that such restrictions are necessary for military readiness and operations.

This ruling comes as part of a larger pattern of legal challenges to Trump administration policies across multiple fronts. The appeals court decision suggests that while the judiciary may restrict some aspects of the transgender military ban, the ultimate resolution of the issue remains uncertain pending potential Supreme Court review.

The divided nature of the appellate panel underscores the contentious nature of the issue, with judges disagreeing about how far the military can go in restricting transgender participation. The majority's focus on calling the ban arbitrary and based on animus indicates concerns about the motivations behind the policy, even as the court allowed restrictions on new enlistment to remain in place.

For active transgender troops currently serving, the ruling provides protection against involuntary discharge based on the Hegseth policy. However, the decision leaves unresolved the question of whether new transgender recruits can be denied entry to the military based on gender identity.

Legal observers note that the path to the Supreme Court appears likely given the administration's stated intent to appeal and the constitutional questions at stake. The high court's eventual ruling could have far-reaching implications for military policy and transgender rights more broadly.

cards.headline: Trump confronts Netanyahu over Lebanon military campaign in heated call
cards.teaser: The president called the Israeli prime minister "crazy" and accused him of ingratitude during an intense phone conversation.
cards.body:
President Trump took Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to task during a phone call over Israel's military operations in Lebanon. According to reporting by Axios, Trump called Netanyahu to express his frustration with the campaign, asking him directly, "What the f--- are you doing?" and accusing him of ingratitude.

The heated exchange underscores rising tensions between the White House and Israeli leadership over how military operations in Lebanon are being conducted. The call comes as Trump attempts to negotiate a ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah, while Iran has suspended talks with the U.S. in protest of Israeli actions in southern Lebanon and Gaza.

cards.headline: Anthropic Files for Initial Public Offering
cards.teaser: The artificial intelligence company has filed paperwork to go public in what could become one of the largest technology debuts in years.
cards.body:
Anthropic has filed confidentially for an initial public offering on the US stock market. The company, which develops the Claude chatbot used by software engineers and business clients, announced the move on Monday without disclosing its target valuation or other offering terms.

The timing reflects Anthropic's rapid ascent in the AI sector. The company raised $65 billion in funding this year, valuing it at $965 billion, up from a $380 billion valuation just months earlier. The potential IPO could rank among the largest in US history and bring AI investment opportunities to millions of Americans with retirement accounts.

cards.headline: Alphabet Plans to Raise $80 Billion for AI Infrastructure
cards.teaser: Google's parent company will sell stock to fund a massive buildout of artificial intelligence computing capacity.
cards.body:
Alphabet announced plans to raise $80 billion through stock sales to fund its artificial intelligence infrastructure expansion. The company cited strong demand for its AI solutions from enterprises and consumers, with demand currently exceeding its available supply. The proceeds will support expansion of data centers and acquisition of specialized chips and equipment needed to train and operate large AI models.

This capital raise underscores the substantial investment required to build competitive AI computing systems. The move comes as multiple AI-focused companies prepare for initial public offerings, intensifying competition for investor capital in the technology sector.

cards.headline: Explosion kills dozens at rebel warehouse in Myanmar village
cards.teaser: Local authorities said the blast at a warehouse holding mining explosives was an accident.
cards.body:
Dozens of people were killed when an explosion flattened a village in rebel-held territory in Myanmar. Local authorities attributed the blast to an accident at a warehouse that stored explosives used for mining operations.

The explosion destroyed structures across the village, causing widespread destruction in the rebel-controlled area. Authorities said the warehouse contained explosives intended for mining, which detonated in what they described as an accidental blast.

cards.headline: Israel captures historic Beaufort Castle in southern Lebanon
cards.teaser: Israeli forces seized the ancient crusader fortress as part of their incursion into southern Lebanon.
cards.body:
Israeli forces took control of Beaufort Castle, a historic crusader fortress in southern Lebanon, as part of ongoing military operations in the region. The capture of the ancient stronghold marked a significant development in the conflict.

Following the seizure, ceasefire efforts have accelerated. Lebanon announced that Hezbollah agreed to a reciprocal halt to attacks on Israel. However, hours after the pause was announced, the Israeli military said it intercepted projectiles fired from Lebanon. The U.N. Security Council called for Israel to withdraw from southern Lebanon, while President Trump stated that Israel and Hezbollah had agreed not to attack each other.

cards.headline: Colombia presidential election heads to runoff
cards.teaser: Candidate Abelardo de la Espriella will face a left-wing senator in a June runoff election.
cards.body:
Colombia's presidential election will proceed to a runoff on June 21 after no candidate won a majority in the first round. Far-right lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, a Trump admirer, secured 43.7% of the vote, narrowly edging left-wing senator Iván Cepeda, who received 40.9%. Cepeda, a philosopher and human rights activist serving since 2014, is backed by departing President Gustavo Petro.

The runoff has triggered mixed reactions across Colombian society. The election could significantly reshape Colombia's relationship with the United States, with the two candidates representing starkly different political visions and international orientations.

cards.headline: European Union approves strict migration law allowing deportation centers outside bloc
cards.teaser: The EU reached a deal on what officials called the strictest-ever migration law, including provisions for return hubs.
cards.body:
The European Union approved new migration legislation that allows member states to deport migrants to processing centers located outside the bloc. The Council and Parliament reached an agreement on returns of illegally staying third-country nationals, paving the way for the new deportation procedures.

The law represents the EU's strictest approach to migration policy and reflects hardening views across Europe on how to handle migrants. The agreement includes provisions for return hubs and fast-track deportation processes for individuals without legal permission to remain in EU countries.

cards.headline: Denmark's Mette Frederiksen to form coalition government
cards.teaser: The Social Democratic Party leader will serve a third term as prime minister after months of negotiations.
cards.body:
Denmark's Mette Frederiksen, leader of the Social Democratic Party, has agreed to form a centre-left coalition minority government, securing her third consecutive term as prime minister. The coalition deal concludes months of political uncertainty following the March election.

The agreement comes amid a broader crisis in Denmark's relationship with the United States over Greenland. The new minority cabinet will govern despite not holding a majority in parliament, where 12 parties won seats in the recent election.

cards.headline: UN Security Council calls for Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon
cards.teaser: The panel met after Israel threatened to attack southern Beirut, though both sides later agreed to pause attacks.
cards.body:
The UN Security Council convened to discuss Israel's military presence in southern Lebanon following Israeli threats against southern Beirut. President Trump announced that Israel and Hezbollah had reached an agreement to cease hostilities against each other.

Lebanon reported that Hezbollah had accepted a reciprocal halt to attacks on Israel. However, shortly after the pause was announced, the Israeli military reported intercepting projectiles fired from Lebanese territory. Prime Minister Netanyahu subsequently distanced himself from ceasefire discussions regarding Lebanon.

cards.headline: Store owner acquitted in shooting death of Black teenager in South Carolina
cards.teaser: A jury found Rick Chow not guilty of murder in the killing of 14-year-old Cyrus Carmack-Belton.
cards.body:
A South Carolina jury acquitted convenience store owner Rick Chow of murder charges in the shooting death of 14-year-old Cyrus Carmack-Belton. The verdict was returned after a trial that drew attention from Court TV and multiple news outlets.

Chow had been charged with murder in the death of the Black teenager. The jury deliberated on the case and determined that the prosecution had not proven murder beyond a reasonable doubt. The acquittal concludes the criminal case against Chow in the shooting.

cards.headline: Democrats express concern over Maine Senate candidate ahead of primary
cards.teaser: Graham Platner faces scrutiny after reports emerged about sexually explicit texts sent to other women.
cards.body:
Democratic Party officials are expressing anxiety about Senate candidate Graham Platner ahead of the Maine primary election. According to reports, Platner's wife informed his campaign that he had sent sexually explicit texts to other women.

Party leaders worry that Platner's candidacy could damage Democrats not only in Maine but in broader races as well. Platner is scheduled to meet with Senate Democrats to discuss the controversy.

cards.headline: North Carolina officer charged with assault after video shows him punching woman during arrest
cards.teaser: A former Shelby police officer turned himself in to face criminal charges after being fired over the incident.
cards.body:
A North Carolina police officer turned himself in to face assault charges following a violent arrest captured on video. The officer, who was fired from the Shelby Police Department, was shown repeatedly striking a Black woman during the incident. The video circulated widely across news outlets including CBS News.

The officer's termination came after the footage of the arrest surfaced publicly. He now faces criminal assault charges related to his conduct during the encounter.

cards.headline: Three people killed in Sandy shooting, suspect named in court documents
cards.teaser: A kidnapping charge has been added against the suspect in the Oregon shooting.
cards.body:
Court documents have identified the suspect and three victims in a shooting that occurred in Sandy, Oregon. The filing revealed new details about the case, including the names of those killed.

Authorities have added a kidnapping charge against the suspect in addition to other charges stemming from the incident, indicating multiple criminal allegations arising from the same event.

cards.headline: Israeli military intercepts projectiles from Lebanon after halt to attacks announced
cards.teaser: Lebanon said Hezbollah agreed to a reciprocal pause in strikes, but Israeli forces later detected incoming fire.
cards.body:
Lebanese officials announced that Hezbollah agreed to a reciprocal halt to attacks on Israel. However, the Israeli military said it intercepted projectiles fired from Lebanon shortly after the pause was announced.

Trump stated that Israel and Hezbollah would stop fighting. The announcement came as Iran broke off ceasefire talks with the U.S. over Israeli operations in Lebanon and Gaza.

cards.headline: Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv kill at least five people
cards.teaser: Thousands of residents sought shelter after officials reported strikes on the city center.
cards.body:
Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's capital overnight killed at least five people. The attacks targeted Kyiv's city center, forcing thousands of residents to seek shelter as sirens warned of the incoming strikes.

The overnight bombardment marks the latest in a series of Russian attacks on civilian areas in the Ukrainian capital.

cards.headline: Berkshire Hathaway Invests $16.8 Billion in Two Days Under New CEO
cards.teaser: Greg Abel, who recently took over as chief executive, has overseen major acquisitions including an $8.5 billion purchase of homebuilder Taylor Morrison.
cards.body:
Berkshire Hathaway deployed $16.8 billion in capital over two days under new CEO Greg Abel, including an $8.5 billion acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison. The investment spree marks a significant shift for the conglomerate, which had maintained a substantial cash position.

Abel's early moves signal a willingness to deploy capital into sectors including housing construction, demonstrating a change in strategy as he takes leadership of Berkshire.

cards.headline: Alphabet Plans to Raise $80 Billion for AI Infrastructure
cards.teaser: Google's parent company will sell stock to fund a massive buildout of artificial intelligence computing capacity.
cards.body:
Alphabet announced plans to raise $80 billion through stock sales to fund its artificial intelligence infrastructure expansion. The company cited strong demand for its AI solutions from enterprises and consumers, with demand currently exceeding its available supply. The proceeds will support expansion of data centers and acquisition of specialized chips and equipment needed to train and operate large AI models.

This capital raise underscores the substantial investment required to build competitive AI computing systems. The move comes as multiple AI-focused companies prepare for initial public offerings, intensifying competition for investor capital in the technology sector.

cards.headline: Short Seller Andrew Left Convicted of Securities Fraud
cards.teaser: The prominent investor known for critical research reports on public companies has been found guilty of fraud charges.
cards.body:
A jury found short seller Andrew Left guilty of securities fraud charges. Left gained prominence for publishing research reports questioning the valuations and business practices of public companies, often taking short positions that would profit if share prices declined.

The conviction marks a significant legal outcome for a figure who played a visible role in financial markets for years. Left faced allegations related to his trading activity and public statements about companies he researched.

cards.headline: HPE Shares Surge 30% on Server Demand Driven by AI
cards.teaser: Hewlett Packard Enterprise reported record results as companies buy networking equipment to support artificial intelligence systems.
cards.body:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise shares jumped 30% after the company posted its largest earnings beat since 2018, driven by strong demand for servers and networking equipment. The results reflected growing corporate spending on infrastructure needed to deploy AI applications, with HPE saying it expects to reach financial targets set for 2028 as early as this year.

The earnings report showed AI-related sales generating significant revenue growth across HPE's product lines. Companies building out data centers and AI capabilities have turned to established hardware providers like HPE for the servers and networking gear required to run large-scale computing operations.

cards.headline: Blue Origin Launchpad Repairs May Take Until 2028
cards.teaser: NASA's administrator says the facility damaged in a rocket explosion will require extensive reconstruction work.
cards.body:
A Blue Origin New Glenn rocket exploded on its launch pad at Cape Canaveral, Florida on Thursday night during a test. The damage to the launch complex was substantial, with debris scattered across the surrounding area and potentially reaching Florida beaches.

According to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, repairs to the facility could take until 2028. The extensive damage will require significant time and resources to restore the launchpad to operational status.

hero.headline: NASA confirms meteor explosion over northeastern US with force of 230 tons of TNT
hero.body:
NASA has confirmed that a meteor exploded over the northeastern United States during the weekend, with a blast force equivalent to 230 tons of TNT. The fireball prompted reports of loud booms and sightings from Delaware to Montreal.

The meteor was approximately 3 feet wide as it entered Earth's atmosphere near the New Hampshire and Massachusetts border, north of Boston. Residents across the region reported hearing loud booms or witnessing the bright fireball streaking across the sky before the explosion occurred.

According to NASA's statement, the meteor became visible at 49 miles above Stagecoach, northwest of Houston. It traveled southeast at 35,000 miles per hour before breaking apart 29 miles above Bammel, just west of Cypress Station. The fragmentation of the meteor created a pressure wave that produced the audible booms heard by people in the area.

The American Meteor Society confirmed the event, noting that this type of occurrence is exceptionally rare. Eyewitness accounts came from multiple states and extended into Canada, with sightings reported as far north as Montreal.

Meteors of this size entering Earth's atmosphere are uncommon events. When they do occur, friction generated by passing through the atmosphere at high speeds causes them to heat up and often break apart or explode before reaching the ground. The energy released in such explosions can be substantial, as demonstrated by the equivalent force in this case.

NASA's confirmation provides scientific validation of the numerous eyewitness accounts from across the northeastern region. The agency's ability to calculate the explosive force indicates sophisticated monitoring systems tracked the meteor's entry and destruction.

This recent event comes amid a series of meteor sightings across North America. Just days before the northeastern explosion, a meteor in Ohio created a sonic boom heard as far away as Pennsylvania. That asteroid, measuring about 2 meters in diameter and weighing approximately 6 tons, traveled at 45,000 miles per hour.

Additionally, a suspected meteorite crashed into a home in suburban Houston on Saturday evening. A local resident reported finding a hole in the ceiling and discovering what appeared to be a meteor inside. The fire department received multiple reports of a meteor that had exploded into multiple pieces over the northern Houston area.

While spectacular to witness, such events typically pose little danger to populated areas. The northeastern explosion occurred over water, which likely minimized any potential ground impact or damage. However, the Houston incident demonstrates that meteorites can occasionally strike residential areas, making these events noteworthy for both scientists and the general public who experience them.

cards.headline: Alphabet plans to raise $80 billion for AI infrastructure
cards.teaser: The company says demand for its AI solutions from enterprises and consumers exceeds available supply.
cards.body:
Alphabet announced plans to raise $80 billion to fund its artificial intelligence infrastructure expansion. The company cited strong demand for its AI solutions and services from both enterprises and consumers, with demand currently exceeding its available supply.

The capital will support the company's buildout of AI infrastructure, including the data centers, computing hardware, and energy resources required to scale operations and meet market demand for its AI products and services.

cards.headline: Nvidia enters PC market with new Arm-based chip for AI laptops
cards.teaser: Microsoft, Dell, and HP will launch laptops featuring Nvidia's first PC processors designed for AI agents.
cards.body:
Nvidia has launched its RTX Spark superchip, marking its entry into the PC processor market where it will compete against Intel, Apple, Qualcomm, and AMD. The chip is designed to bring AI agent capabilities to laptops and desktop computers, potentially replacing traditional mouse and keyboard interactions. Microsoft, Dell, and HP have announced devices featuring the new processor.

The move represents Nvidia's expansion from its dominant position in AI server chips into consumer computing. The $5 trillion semiconductor company is positioning the technology to make AI agents accessible to mainstream users, entering the $200 billion CPU market with what analysts suggest could be a significant opportunity if the company has successfully made AI agents practical and useful for consumers.

cards.headline: Defense tech company Mach Industries reaches $1.8 billion valuation
cards.teaser: The startup raised $300 million in new funding, quadrupling its valuation in a year.
cards.body:
Mach Industries raised $300 million in new funding, bringing its valuation to $1.8 billion. The defense technology company quadrupled its valuation in just one year under 22-year-old founder and CEO Ethan Thornton.

The company has five autonomous vehicles in development and recently completed a major acquisition, demonstrating rapid expansion in the defense technology sector.

cards.headline: Moderna receives $50 million to develop mRNA Ebola vaccine
cards.teaser: The funding aims to accelerate development of a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain amid an active outbreak.
cards.body:
Moderna received $50 million in funding to develop an mRNA vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola virus. The investment comes as health officials work to urgently accelerate vaccine development during an active Ebola outbreak.

The funding builds on the proven success of mRNA vaccine technology demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic. Moderna will apply its mRNA platform to create a vaccine targeting Bundibugyo, one of several Ebola virus strains that causes severe disease in humans.

cards.headline: GitHub Copilot users hit monthly credit limits in single day under new pricing
cards.teaser: Users report burning through their entire monthly AI credit allotment in one day after GitHub switched to usage-based pricing.
cards.body:
GitHub Copilot users are reacting to a new usage-based pricing system that replaced previous subscription models. Some users report burning through their whole monthly AI credit allotment in a single day of use.

The pricing change has prompted questions about the actual cost of AI-assisted coding tools. Users expressed surprise at how quickly credits were consumed during typical development workflows, raising concerns about the long-term affordability of AI coding assistants for individual developers and small teams.

cards.headline: Hackers stole celebrity Instagram accounts by exploiting Meta AI chatbot
cards.teaser: Attackers duped Meta's AI support system to gain access to valuable Instagram handles before the exploit was patched.
cards.body:
Hackers exploited Meta's AI support chatbot to gain unauthorized access to high-profile Instagram accounts, including Barack Obama's White House account, Sephora, and the US Space Force Chief Master Sergeant. The attackers manipulated the automated system into granting account access, bypassing normal security measures.

Meta confirmed the breach after researchers exposed the vulnerability and subsequently patched the exploit. The incident underscores risks associated with relying on AI chatbots for sensitive security functions like account recovery, as they can be vulnerable to social engineering attacks without proper safeguards.

hero.headline: Hall of Fame basketball coach Rick Adelman dies at 79
hero.body:
Rick Adelman, a Hall of Fame basketball coach who led teams for more than two decades in the NBA, died at 79. Adelman built a reputation as one of the league's most respected coaches through stints with multiple franchises, including the Portland Trail Blazers and Sacramento Kings.

Adelman's coaching career spanned from the late 1980s through the 2010s, during which he became known for his offensive systems and player development. He guided the Trail Blazers to multiple playoff appearances and deep postseason runs, establishing himself as one of the franchise's most successful coaches. His teams were characterized by ball movement and teamwork rather than reliance on individual stars.

The Kings period represented some of Adelman's finest work, as he transformed Sacramento into one of the most exciting teams in basketball during the early 2000s. His coaching philosophy emphasized pace, spacing, and unselfish play, which became influential across the league. Adelman finished his career with over 1,000 regular season victories, placing him among the winningest coaches in NBA history.

Adelman was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in recognition of his sustained excellence and contributions to the sport. Beyond his tactical acumen, he was respected for his calm demeanor and ability to manage diverse personalities in the locker room. His coaching tree influenced numerous assistants who went on to lead their own teams.

The basketball community mourned Adelman's passing, with former players and colleagues remembering his impact on their careers and the game itself. His legacy extends beyond wins and losses to the style of basketball he championed and the professionals he mentored throughout his decades in coaching.

cards.headline: Eagles trade wide receiver A.J. Brown to Patriots
cards.teaser: The Philadelphia Eagles traded wide receiver A.J. Brown to the New England Patriots in exchange for two draft picks.
cards.body:
The Philadelphia Eagles traded wide receiver A.J. Brown to the New England Patriots on Monday, ending months of speculation about his future. The Eagles will receive a first-round pick in 2028 and a fifth-round pick in 2027 in return for the three-time Pro Bowl selection.

The move reunites Brown with Patriots coach Mike Vrabel and comes after Brown grew frustrated during his time in Philadelphia. Both teams announced the deal, marking a significant roster change for the Eagles heading into the upcoming season.

cards.headline: Browns trade Myles Garrett to Rams
cards.teaser: The Cleveland Browns traded defensive end Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams for Jared Verse and three draft picks.
cards.body:
The Cleveland Browns traded star edge rusher Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams for linebacker Jared Verse and three draft picks. Garrett, a 30-year-old two-time Defensive Player of the Year and seven-time Pro Bowl selection, has been one of the league's most productive defensive players since the Browns drafted him first overall in 2017. He holds the record for most sacks (125.5), pressures (413), and tackles for loss (149) since his draft year, and set a single-season sacks record with 23 in 2025.

The trade marks one of the biggest defensive trades in NFL history. Garrett posted a farewell message expressing regret that he could not accomplish more during his time with Cleveland.

cards.headline: Aspiration co-founder Joe Sanberg sentenced to 14 years for fraud
cards.teaser: Joe Sanberg, co-founder of Aspiration Partners, received a 14-year federal prison sentence for fraud.
cards.body:
Joe Sanberg, co-founder of Aspiration Partners, was sentenced to 14 years in federal prison after being convicted of fraud. A federal judge handed down the sentence following the conclusion of the fraud case against the financial services company executive.

The sentencing occurred amid an ongoing NBA investigation involving the Los Angeles Clippers. Aspiration Partners, which Sanberg co-founded, had positioned itself in the financial services sector before the fraud allegations emerged. The 14-year sentence represents a significant penalty in the federal fraud case.

cards.headline: Matteo Berrettini reaches French Open quarterfinals
cards.teaser: Matteo Berrettini advanced to the French Open quarterfinals, his first Grand Slam quarterfinal appearance in nearly four years.
cards.body:
Matteo Berrettini advanced to the French Open quarterfinals after winning his fourth-round match in straight sets. The Italian's progression marks a significant return to the late stages of Grand Slam tournaments following injuries that had sidelined him from reaching quarterfinals since 2022.

Berrettini is among multiple Italian players who made it to the last eight at Roland Garros this year. His comeback underscores a strong resurgence after an extended absence from major tournament success.

cards.headline: Polish qualifier Maja Chwalinska advances to French Open quarterfinals
cards.teaser: Polish qualifier Maja Chwalinska defeated French player Diane Parry to reach the French Open quarterfinals.
cards.body:
Polish qualifier Maja Chwalinska advanced to the French Open quarterfinals by defeating French player Diane Parry. The victory marks an impressive achievement for Chwalinska in her debut at the tournament, as she had to win multiple qualifying matches before entering the main draw.

Chwalinska's run through the bracket has been a standout story of the competition. Despite the home crowd support behind her opponent, the Polish player demonstrated the composure needed to progress through the tournament's early rounds and reach the final eight.

cards.headline: Illinois lawmakers adjourn without passing Bears stadium bill
cards.teaser: The Illinois General Assembly ended its session without passing legislation for a Chicago Bears stadium.
cards.body:
The Illinois House adjourned without voting on a stadium bill that would have provided support for keeping the Chicago Bears in the state. Governor JB Pritzker indicated he was prepared to accept responsibility for a possible Bears departure from Illinois. The General Assembly passed a $55 billion state budget but left the stadium measure unaddressed.

The Bears released a statement following the legislative session's conclusion without action on their stadium proposal. The failure to advance the bill leaves the future of the franchise's location uncertain. Lawmakers ended their session with the stadium question unresolved, creating doubt about whether the team will remain in Illinois.

hero.headline: Marilyn Monroe Fans Gather in Palm Springs for Centennial Birthday Celebration
hero.body:
Fans and impersonators of Marilyn Monroe gathered in Palm Springs to mark what would have been the icon's 100th birthday on June 1. The celebration brought together Monroe lookalikes and admirers to honor the legacy of one of Hollywood's most enduring stars.

Monroe, born Norma Jeane Mortenson in 1926, became one of the most recognizable figures in American cinema during the 1950s and early 1960s. Her films including "Some Like It Hot," "The Seven Year Itch," and "Gentlemen Prefer Blondes" helped establish her as a cultural phenomenon. She died in 1962 at age 36.

Beyond her on-screen presence, Monroe's personal relationships reveal a more complex figure than her public image suggested. According to those who knew her, Monroe maintained deep friendships with both men and women throughout her life. Amy Greene, widow of photographer Milton Greene, shared her home with Monroe during the mid-1950s and described their bond as genuine friendship rather than merely professional association.

Monroe's film roles often reflected female camaraderie. In "Gentlemen Prefer Blondes," she starred alongside Jane Russell, another prominent sex symbol of the era. Despite being paid significantly less than Russell, the two developed a lasting mutual affection that extended beyond their time on set. Years later, Russell reflected on wishing Monroe could have been present at a gathering with close female friends, only to learn of Monroe's death the following day.

Monroe's relationships extended to her professional collaborators, particularly photographers who documented her image. Lawrence Schiller, who worked with Monroe on a notable 1962 photoshoot for her final unfinished film "Something's Got to Give," remembered her as someone with exceptional understanding of photography and lighting. Schiller noted that Monroe took an active role in controlling her image, even destroying negatives she disliked after a session at Schwab's Pharmacy on Sunset Boulevard.

Another significant friendship was with photographer Sam Shaw, known for capturing one of Monroe's most iconic images: the famous shot of her standing above a subway grate in a billowing white dress. Shaw credited Monroe's "elegance and clean sense of fun" in his posthumously published book "Dear Marilyn."

The centennial observance has sparked renewed interest in Monroe's life beyond her film roles and public persona. The Palm Springs gathering featured fans dressed in Monroe's signature style, recreating her most famous looks and celebrating her contributions to film and popular culture. This event underscores how Monroe's legacy has transcended generations, maintaining relevance in contemporary discussions about fame, image, and Hollywood history. Her influence continues to set standards for stardom decades after her death.

cards.headline: Jury Selection Begins in Sean Combs Sex Trafficking Trial
cards.teaser: Jury selection has started in the sex trafficking trial of music producer Sean "Diddy" Combs as prosecutors in Los Angeles review potential new charges.
cards.body:
Jury selection began in Sean Combs' sex trafficking trial as the case moves forward in federal court. The music producer faces criminal charges related to alleged sex trafficking offenses.

The Los Angeles County District Attorney's office is reviewing a new case that could result in additional criminal charges against Combs. Separately, singer Cassie responded to allegations from a man who claimed she and Combs drugged him, releasing a supportive text message he had previously sent her that contradicts his current claims.

cards.headline: Kelly Curtis, Sister of Jamie Lee Curtis, Dies at 69
cards.teaser: Kelly Curtis, the older sister of actor Jamie Lee Curtis, died on May 30 at age 69.
cards.body:
Kelly Curtis, an actor and filmmaker, died on May 30 at age 69. She passed away peacefully in her home, surrounded by nature, according to her younger sister Jamie Lee Curtis.

Jamie Lee Curtis announced her sister's death in a public statement, calling Kelly "talented" and "jaw droppingly beautiful." The two sisters appeared together in the 1983 film Trading Places. Kelly also had roles in Magic Sticks (1987) and The Devil's Daughter (1991).

cards.headline: Sabrina Carpenter Obtains Restraining Order Against Alleged Stalker
cards.teaser: Pop singer Sabrina Carpenter secured a restraining order after what she described as a deeply alarming incident involving an alleged stalker.
cards.body:
Sabrina Carpenter obtained a restraining order against an individual she accuses of stalking, trespassing, and surveillance. The pop star filed court documents describing a pattern of behavior that has caused her severe emotional distress.

In a declaration, Carpenter stated that the alleged stalker's pattern of stalking, trespassing, and surveillance has caused her severe and ongoing emotional distress. The court granted the restraining order based on the evidence presented.

cards.headline: HBO Max Wins Most Trophies at Gotham Television Awards
cards.teaser: HBO Max took home five awards at the Gotham Television Awards, leading all networks despite Netflix entering with the most nominations.
cards.body:
HBO Max collected five trophies at the Gotham Television Awards ceremony held at Cipriani Wall Street in Manhattan. The network led all competitors in wins despite Netflix entering the evening with 22 nominations, the most of any platform.

Netflix finished second in total awards. Tim Robinson, Chase Infiniti, and Michael Shannon won acting prizes at the ceremony. The programs "I Love LA," "Pluribus," and "DTF St. Louis" took top honors in their respective categories. The Gotham Television Awards serve as a precursor to the Emmy Awards scheduled for September.

cards.headline: Former 60 Minutes Producer Criticizes CBS News Leadership
cards.teaser: Bill Owens, former executive producer of 60 Minutes, issued a warning about the direction of the newsmagazine under current CBS News leadership.
cards.body:
Bill Owens, a former executive producer of 60 Minutes, criticized CBS News leadership over changes to the program. His comments came as the network underwent a significant overhaul that included firing the show's executive producer, executive editor, and two correspondents—Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega.

During a staff meeting with newly appointed executive producer Nick Bilton and CBS News managing editor Charles Forelle, veteran correspondent Scott Pelley strongly objected to the cuts, specifically targeting Bari Weiss, the network's editor-in-chief, over her role in the restructuring.

cards.headline: Vanilla Ice Says He Would Perform for Putin and Iran After Artists Drop Out of Freedom 250 Concerts
cards.teaser: Rapper Vanilla Ice said he would perform for anybody, including Putin and Iran, after several artists withdrew from concerts planned for the nation's 250th anniversary celebration.
cards.body:
Vanilla Ice stated he would perform for any audience, including Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iran, after several artists withdrew from the Freedom 250 concert series. The concerts were planned as part of celebrations for the nation's 250th anniversary.

Young MC, Poison frontman Bret Michaels, and country singer Martina McBride dropped out of the event, citing concerns that it would become politically charged. Following the departures, the concert series was rebranded as a Great American State Fair, with the Trump administration set to headline the revised event.

hero.headline: Appeals court blocks Trump transgender military ban as unconstitutional
hero.body:
A federal appeals court ruled on Monday that the Trump administration is unconstitutionally expelling active transgender troops under a policy implemented by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The divided three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for Washington DC delivered a significant legal setback to the administration's efforts to remove transgender service members from the military.

The majority opinion characterized the ban as "arbitrary, and based on animus," according to the court's decision. However, the split ruling also allows the armed services to continue blocking transgender individuals from enlisting in the military, creating a distinction between active duty personnel and new recruits.

The court's decision is expected to face challenges from the government, with legal experts predicting the case will ultimately reach the Supreme Court. The ruling represents a complex outcome that restricts the scope of the administration's transgender military policy while leaving room for future legal battles over enlistment restrictions.

Hegseth responded to the ruling by signaling his intention to appeal to the nation's highest court. In a statement following the decision, he wrote "see you at SCOTUS," indicating his willingness to pursue the case further through the judicial system.

The case has become a focal point in the broader debate over the Trump administration's anti-diversity agenda. Civil liberties advocates have argued that the policy unconstitutionally targets transgender service members, while the administration has maintained that such restrictions are necessary for military readiness and operations.

This ruling comes as part of a larger pattern of legal challenges to Trump administration policies across multiple fronts. The appeals court decision suggests that while the judiciary may restrict some aspects of the transgender military ban, the ultimate resolution of the issue remains uncertain pending potential Supreme Court review.

The divided nature of the appellate panel underscores the contentious nature of the issue, with judges disagreeing about how far the military can go in restricting transgender participation. The majority's focus on calling the ban arbitrary and based on animus indicates concerns about the motivations behind the policy, even as the court allowed restrictions on new enlistment to remain in place.

For active transgender troops currently serving, the ruling provides protection against involuntary discharge based on the Hegseth policy. However, the decision leaves unresolved the question of whether new transgender recruits can be denied entry to the military based on gender identity.

Legal observers note that the path to the Supreme Court appears likely given the administration's stated intent to appeal and the constitutional questions at stake. The high court's eventual ruling could have far-reaching implications for military policy and transgender rights more broadly.

cards.headline: Iran suspends negotiations over Strait of Hormuz amid Lebanon strikes
cards.teaser: Tehran halted talks with Washington after Israeli attacks on Lebanon, dimming prospects for reopening the strategic waterway.
cards.body:
Iran halted talks with the United States over reopening the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, citing Israel's military operations in Lebanon and Gaza as the reason for the suspension. The move came after President Trump had expressed optimism the previous week about brokering a deal with Tehran on the strategic waterway.

Trump has been attempting to negotiate a ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah while simultaneously pushing Iran back to the negotiating table. According to reports, Trump also confronted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by phone over his military campaign in Lebanon, questioning his strategy. The breakdown in negotiations represents a setback for the administration's efforts to resolve both the maritime dispute and the escalating regional conflict.

cards.headline: Trump confronts Netanyahu over Lebanon military campaign in heated call
cards.teaser: The president called the Israeli prime minister "crazy" and accused him of ingratitude during an intense phone conversation.
cards.body:
President Trump took Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to task during a phone call over Israel's military operations in Lebanon. According to reporting by Axios, Trump called Netanyahu to express his frustration with the campaign, asking him directly, "What the f--- are you doing?" and accusing him of ingratitude.

The heated exchange underscores rising tensions between the White House and Israeli leadership over how military operations in Lebanon are being conducted. The call comes as Trump attempts to negotiate a ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah, while Iran has suspended talks with the U.S. in protest of Israeli actions in southern Lebanon and Gaza.

cards.headline: Democrats introduce bill to eliminate Trump anti-weaponization fund
cards.teaser: Three senators proposed legislation to bar taxpayer money from going to payments for Trump associates targeted in prosecutions.
cards.body:
Democratic Senators Mark Kelly of Arizona, Adam Schiff of California, and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan introduced the Drain the Slush Fund Act to block the Trump administration's $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund. The legislation would prevent taxpayer money from being used for payments to the president and his associates.

The fund, created through a settlement with the IRS, has faced significant legal and political challenges since its announcement two weeks prior. More than a dozen Republican senators have urged the administration to reconsider the program, and polling shows majorities of both Democrats and Republicans oppose it.

cards.headline: Maine Democratic Senate candidate faces questions over messages to women
cards.teaser: Graham Platner will meet with Senate Democrats as reports surface about sexually explicit communications sent after his marriage.
cards.body:
Graham Platner, the Democratic Senate candidate in Maine, is scheduled to meet with Senate Democrats. The meeting comes after media reports that he sent sexually explicit messages to multiple women after he married his wife. A campaign official described the meeting as longstanding and not arranged in response to the allegations.

The Maine Democratic primary is eight days away, putting Democrats in a difficult position after Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer backed Platner over Governor Janet Mills. Senator Bernie Sanders defended Platner and told reporters he is not rethinking his endorsement, saying the candidate is getting through marriage problems.

cards.headline: Republican senators remain skeptical of Justice Department fund reversal
cards.teaser: GOP lawmakers say Trump must explicitly rule out reviving the anti-weaponization compensation program.
cards.body:
Republican senators are pressing for explicit assurances that the Trump administration will not pursue an "anti-weaponization" fund. Senator Chuck Grassley emphasized the need for a clear presidential statement ruling out such a mechanism going forward.

The $1.8 billion fund, created through an out-of-court settlement in Trump v. the IRS, faced widespread criticism from both parties. A court order has paused the program, though the Justice Department has stated it "strongly disagrees" with the ruling while pledging to comply. Polling showed majorities of Democrats and Republicans oppose the fund, while more than a dozen Republican senators urged the administration to abandon the initiative.

cards.headline: House Democrats monitor California primaries as test of anti-incumbent mood
cards.teaser: Multiple longtime Democratic representatives in their 70s and 80s face challenges from younger candidates.
cards.body:
House Democrats are watching California's primary elections as a measure of anti-incumbency sentiment among voters. Democratic Representatives Mike Thompson, Doris Matsui, and Brad Sherman, all age 70 or older, face primary challenges from younger Democrats who have criticized their lengthy tenures in Congress.

The primaries represent the first significant test of whether Democratic voters will reject long-serving members in favor of new candidates. Democratic colleagues are closely monitoring the races to gauge whether age and tenure have become liabilities for sitting members, potentially signaling broader concerns about the party's leadership structure.
